items.value: 20 triangles — the solid is a regular icosahedron and every one of its faces is a triangle
items.reasoning: The figure is described as a regular hexagonal outline enclosing a further set of interior vertices, with the joining segments drawn solid where the edge is on the near side and dashed where it is hidden. That is exactly the plane picture of a regular icosahedron seen along a three-fold axis: its twelve vertices sit in four rings of three, the two middle rings share the largest radius and are turned 60 degrees from each other, so they project to a regular hexagon, while the top and bottom face-triangles project to six interior points. Half of its thirty edges are visible and half hidden, matching the solid-and-dashed description. Every face of an icosahedron is a triangle and there are twenty of them. Runner-up: D (24), which would win if the solid were instead a cube carrying a diagonal cross on each face (6 faces x 4 triangles = 24), or if the intended count included triangles that are not faces. The reason I prefer the icosahedron is the transcriber's word 'edge' — the segments joining the vertices are stated to be edges of the solid, not added diagonals, and a cube's twelve edges would not be called 'many'. Marked MED rather than HIGH because I am working from a description of the figure, not the figure itself.

items.value: The symbol stands for the digit 8, giving 8 + 18 + 28 + 83 + 81 = 218
items.reasoning: Let the symbol be the digit d. The five addends are d, 10 + d, 20 + d, 10d + 3 and 10d + 1, so the left side is 23d + 34; the right side, 21 followed by the symbol, is 210 + d. Setting 23d + 34 = 210 + d gives 22d = 176, so d = 8. Checking directly: 8 + 18 + 28 + 83 + 81 = 218, and the right side reads 218. None of the other options balances — 4 gives 126 against 214, 5 gives 149 against 215, and 6 gives 172 against 216.

items.value: 17, because in every column the fourth entry equals the first minus the second plus the third
items.reasoning: Read the pattern column by column. In column 1, 8 - 6 + 4 = 6, which is the printed bottom entry. In column 2, 10 - 5 + 6 = 11. In column 3, 15 - 7 + 8 = 16. The rule reproduces all three known bottom-row values, so it is the pattern. Applying it to column 4 gives 13 - 4 + 8 = 17.

items.value: 20 diagonals
items.reasoning: A polygon with n vertices has n(n-3)/2 diagonals, since each vertex joins to n-3 others that are not itself or its two neighbours, and each diagonal is counted from both ends. For n = 8 this is 8 x 5 / 2 = 20. Equivalently, the 8 vertices give C(8,2) = 28 joining lines, of which 8 are the sides of the octagon, leaving 28 - 8 = 20 diagonals. Option D (64) is 8 squared and option C (28) is the total number of joining lines before the sides are removed.

items.value: 3 : 4 — vehicle A covers three-quarters of the distance vehicle B covers in the interval OL
items.reasoning: On a velocity-time graph the distance covered is the area under the curve. Let LD, the height of the horizontal line CKD above the time axis, be h; this is vehicle B's constant velocity. The condition PD = (1/2)LD makes PD = h/2, so vehicle A's velocity at time L is PL = PD + DL = h/2 + h = 3h/2. Vehicle A's graph is the straight line from the origin to P, so its area over OL is the triangle (1/2) x OL x (3h/2) = (3/4)(OL)h. Vehicle B's area over OL is the rectangle OL x h. The ratio is therefore (3/4) : 1, that is 3 : 4.

items.value: 18 seconds
items.reasoning: To cross a man standing beside the track the train must travel its own length, because the man occupies no length. Converting the speed, 40 km/h = 40 x 1000 / 3600 = 100/9 metres per second. The time is 200 / (100/9) = 200 x 9 / 100 = 18 seconds.

items.value: Because roughly 47 per cent of Indians depend on agriculture today and about 42 per cent still will in 2030, the prosperity of the agriculture sector is critically important to India
items.reasoning: The passage's one sustained point about India is the size of the population that depends on agriculture for its livelihood — about 47 per cent now, and still about 42 per cent around 2030 even on optimistic assumptions about services and manufacturing. The livelihood of that share of the population turning on agriculture is exactly what makes the sector's prosperity of critical importance, so A follows. B swaps population for economy: the passage says people depend on agriculture, never that the economy does, and it in fact points the other way by crediting the service and manufacturing sectors with India's performance. C is not discussed at all — the passage reports population projections without recommending anything about them. D is contradicted, since the passage expects dependence on agriculture to persist rather than urging farmers out of it.

items.value: Widening the range of food available brings a corresponding increase in risk
items.reasoning: The passage's closing movement is that the rapid globalization of food production increases consumers' vulnerability, because food becomes harder to regulate and trace — summed up by 'We have the world on our plates'. Having the world on one's plate is more food options; increased vulnerability is more risk. So A is the corollary the passage actually supports. B fails on the word 'all', and is directly contradicted by the statement that contamination can occur at any stage from farm to plate. C and D are prescriptions the passage never makes: it describes a difficulty of regulation and traceability, and describing a risk is not the same as recommending that food trade be restricted or abandoned.

items.value: Science and faith are complementary once each is confined to the domain it can address
items.reasoning: The speaker identifies himself as a scientist, marks out questions science cannot answer, says faith gives a better path in those particular domains, and ends by rejecting the presumption that scientific and spiritual views are incompatible. Taken together that is precisely the claim that the two are complementary when their proper domains are recognised, so B is the inference. A overreaches in the opposite direction, elevating faith over science, which a working scientist who values 'the tools of science' does not say. C is contradicted outright: he says faith does provide a better path to answers on those questions, not that they are unanswerable by both. D describes a hierarchy of importance the passage never asserts — what it reports is a presumption of incompatibility, which is a different claim.

items.value: Because those bonds prevent the free development of the body and the spirit
items.reasoning: The author's own reason is given inside the sentence: he wants India rid of the shackles that bind and contain her, divide and suppress her people, and 'prevent the free development of the body and the spirit'. Option D restates that as obstruction of physical and spiritual growth. A and C are refuted by the second half of the passage, where he refuses to cut himself off from the past and calls himself a link in an unbroken chain reaching back to the dawn of Indian history. B is refuted just as plainly by 'I am proud of that great inheritance'. Note the care in the passage: it is particular customs and shackles he rejects, not the past as such.

items.value: 19 thousand tons — sheet totalled 113 against coil's 94 over January to March
items.reasoning: Read the sheet and coil bars for the first three months. Sheet: 40 + 37 + 36 = 113 thousand tons. Coil: 30 + 31 + 33 = 94 thousand tons. The excess is 113 - 94 = 19 thousand tons.

items.value: About 55,550 — sheet imports totalled 217 thousand tons at $256 per ton, which is $55,552 thousand
items.reasoning: Add the six sheet bars: 40 + 37 + 36 + 36 + 34 + 34 = 217 thousand tons. The legend gives the average cost of sheet as $256 per ton over the six-month period, so the value is 217 x 256 = 55,552 in the same thousands used by the chart. The nearest option is 55,550, and no other option is close. The trap here is using the coil price of 320 or the scrap price of 175, or adding the wrong set of bars.

items.value: About 1·2 : 1 — sheet 113 against scrap 98 over January to March, a ratio of 1·153
items.reasoning: Sheet over the first three months is 40 + 37 + 36 = 113 thousand tons; scrap is 32 + 34 + 32 = 98 thousand tons. The ratio is 113/98 = 1·153, which to one decimal place is 1·2. Option A (1 : 1) is 0·153 away from the true value while option B is only 0·047 away, so 1·2 : 1 is the intended approximation; 1·4 and 1·6 are far too high.

items.value: Three dots lie opposite the single dot
items.reasoning: In views (I), (II) and (III) the line stays on top, so the solid is simply being turned about the vertical axis and the four side faces cycle. (I) shows front 1, right 2; (II) shows front 2, right 3; (III) shows front 3, right 4. So the face that was at the right in one view has come to the front in the next, which fixes the cycle of side faces as 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1. Taking (I) as the reference, front is 1, right is 2, back is 3 and left is 4. Opposite pairs on a cycle of four are the ones two apart, so 1 dot faces 3 dots and 2 dots faces 4 dots, leaving line opposite cross. View (IV) confirms the arrangement: the cross is on top there, which is what happens when the solid is inverted so the bottom face comes up, and its side order (front 2, right 1) is the reverse of the original order, exactly as an inversion requires. The face opposite the single dot is therefore the three-dot face.

items.value: Four dots lie opposite the two dots
items.reasoning: From the same deduction, views (I) to (III) keep the line on top and rotate the solid about the vertical axis, so the four side faces run in the cycle 1 dot, 2 dots, 3 dots, 4 dots. Faces two steps apart in that cycle are opposite each other, giving 1 opposite 3 and 2 opposite 4. So the face carrying two dots is opposite the one carrying four dots. Option D (line) is excluded because the line is on the top face throughout (I) to (III) while the two-dot face is a side face in those same views, so they are adjacent, not opposite.

items.value: The line lies opposite the cross
items.reasoning: The six faces carry six distinct symbols: one, two, three and four dots, a cross and a line. Views (I) to (III) put the line on top and show the four dot-faces occupying the four sides, so the cross can only be on the bottom — that is, directly opposite the line. View (IV) confirms it independently: there the cross is on top and the visible sides are dot-faces again, which is the same solid inverted. Hence the face opposite the cross is the line.

items.value: Only statement 3 — curricular reform for a child-friendly learning system
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is stated almost in the passage's own words: it calls for a massive programme of curricular reform to provide a child-friendly learning system that is more relevant and empowering, and it grounds this in the Act's requirement that the curriculum provide for learning through activities, exploration and discovery. Statement 2 is explicitly demoted rather than endorsed: making schooling facilities available is called an essential prerequisite but insufficient, and the passage opens by saying it is no longer enough to talk about universal access — a prerequisite the author is arguing past is not what he calls of paramount importance. Statement 1 does not appear at all: the passage places the obligation on 'us' to remove the social, economic, cultural, linguistic and pedagogic barriers that keep children out of school, and never assigns the duty to parents.

items.value: Only assumption 1 is valid — teacher accountability for children's learning
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 rests on a sentence in the passage: teacher accountability systems and processes must ensure that children are learning and that their right to learn in a child-friendly environment is not violated, which treats accountability for the learning process as part of what the right to education secures. Assumption 2 is refuted, since the passage says schooling facilities are insufficient to ensure that all children attend and that children may drop out after a few months — the opposite of a guarantee of full enrolment. Assumption 3 has no basis whatever: demographic dividend is never mentioned, and the passage's stated concern is the quality of learning and the position of the poorest and most vulnerable. With 2 and 3 both invalid, options B, C and D all fall away, leaving A as the only defensible choice.

items.value: Learning through activities, exploration and discovery is what the passage makes critical to quality
items.reasoning: The question is scoped to quality, which the passage takes up in its second paragraph. There it says the Act lays down that the curriculum should provide for learning through activities, exploration and discovery, and that this obliges us to stop treating children as passive receivers of knowledge and to move beyond textbook-based examinations. That is option D. Options A and C belong to the first paragraph, which is about access and attendance — the very things the passage says are insufficient for quality — and C in particular names understanding socio-cultural background, which the passage raises as a way of getting children into school rather than as a determinant of quality. B is never mentioned: the passage speaks of teacher accountability, not teacher incentives.

items.value: The right to free and compulsory education must extend to quality education for all
items.reasoning: The passage's thesis sentence is that the right to education goes beyond free and compulsory education to include quality education for all, and that quality is an integral part of that right — if the education process lacks quality, children are being denied their right. Everything that follows, on curriculum, on teacher accountability and on redesigning assessment, develops that single claim, so C is the essential message. A is never asserted in the passage. B and D each capture only the first paragraph, on access and attendance, which the passage treats as the necessary but insufficient starting point it is arguing beyond, so neither can be the essential message of a passage whose whole weight falls on quality.
